Segal's Gamma rings
Compute the extension of the field with one element $\mathbb{F}_1$ to $\mathbb{Z}$ via Borger's $\Lambda$-rings
https://alainconnes.org/wp-content/uploads/segals-GammaRings.pdf
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(1) To organise Galois groups and modules, how does one formulate a classical class formation?
Hint
A class formation is a pair $(\Gamma, A)$ where $\Gamma$ is a profinite group and $A$ is a discrete $\Gamma$-module such that for every open subgroup $H \subset \Gamma$ and open normal subgroup $N \triangleleft H$, $H^1(H/N, A^N) = 0$ and $H^2(H/N, A^N) \cong \frac{1}{[H:N]}\mathbb{Z}/\mathbb{Z}$ canonically via an invariant map $\mathrm{inv}_{H/N}$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(2) How does one establish the vanishing of $H^1(H/N, A^N)$ and the cyclicity of $H^2(H/N, A^N)$?
Hint
By studying the Galois fixed-point modules $A^N$ across finite Galois extensions and computing the Herbrand quotient $h(A^N) = [H:N]$ for cyclic steps using Hilbert's Theorem 90 for the $H^1$-vanishing.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(3) What is the purpose of the Nakayama-Tate lemma in class formations?
Hint
Given a class formation with fundamental class $\alpha \in H^2(G, A)$, cup product with $\alpha$ yields an isomorphism $\widehat{H}^i(G, \mathbb{Z}) \xrightarrow{\sim} \widehat{H}^{i+2}(G, A)$ for all $i \in \mathbb{Z}$; taking $i = -2$ gives the Artin reciprocity isomorphism $(G)^{\mathrm{ab}} \cong \widehat{H}^{-2}(G, \mathbb{Z}) \xrightarrow{\sim} \widehat{H}^0(G, A) = A^G / \mathrm{Tr}_G(A)$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(4) How does one verify that a given Galois module satisfies the Nakayama-Tate condition?
Hint
Check that for every Sylow $p$-subgroup $G_p \subset G$, $H^1(G_p, A) = 0$ and $H^2(G_p, A)$ is cyclic of order $|G_p|$, generated by the restriction of the fundamental class $\alpha$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(5) How does one construct the Artin reciprocity map with dense image and determine its kernel?
Hint
Taking the projective limit over all open normal subgroups $N \triangleleft H$ of the Nakayama-Tate isomorphisms $(H/N)^{\mathrm{ab}} \cong A^H / \mathrm{Tr}_{H/N}(A^N)$ yields the Artin map $A^H \to H^{\mathrm{ab}}$ with dense image and kernel $\bigcap_{N} \mathrm{Tr}_{H/N}(A^N)$, which is the subgroup of universal norms.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(6) What is the image of the global/local Artin map $A^H \to H^{\mathrm{ab}}$?
Hint
The image is dense in $H^{\mathrm{ab}}$, and the map induces a topological isomorphism $\widehat{A^H} \xrightarrow{\sim} H^{\mathrm{ab}}$ on the appropriate completion (the profinite completion for local fields / idèle class groups).
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(7) What are the axiomatic cohomological criteria required for a class formation?
Hint
(i) $H^1(H/N, A^N) = 0$; (ii) there exists an isomorphism $\mathrm{inv}_{H/N} \colon H^2(H/N, A^N) \xrightarrow{\sim} \frac{1}{[H:N]}\mathbb{Z}/\mathbb{Z}$; (iii) these invariant maps commute with inflation and restriction maps across all open subgroups $N \subset H \subset \Gamma$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(8) How does one reduce the verification of class formation axioms to cyclic extensions?
Hint
By Sylow theory and solvable filtration, any finite group can be decomposed into a tower of cyclic extensions of prime degree; checking the axioms on prime-degree cyclic steps implies them for all finite Galois extensions.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(9) How is Tate cohomology exploited via 2-periodicity for cyclic groups?
Hint
For cyclic $G$, $\widehat{H}^{i}(G, A) \cong \widehat{H}^{i+2}(G, A)$ for all $i$, so the entire cohomology is determined by $\widehat{H}^0(G, A) = A^G / \mathrm{Nm}(A)$ and $\widehat{H}^1(G, A) = \ker(\mathrm{Nm}) / I_G A$, simplifying all calculations to the Herbrand quotient $h(A) = |\widehat{H}^0(A)| / |\widehat{H}^1(A)|$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(10) What ingredients are required to show a module forms a class formation?
Hint
One needs: (1) vanishing of $H^1$ via Hilbert's Theorem 90 / Kummer theory; (2) computation of Herbrand quotients $h(A^N) = [H:N]$; (3) existence of enough cyclic extensions (especially unramified ones) to normalize and assemble the invariant maps.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(11) How is local class field theory proved using class formations for nonarchimedean local fields?
Hint
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be the Galois category of finite separable extensions of $K$, with coefficient functor $A(L) = L^\times$. (1) $H^1(L/K, L^\times) = 0$ by Hilbert 90; (2) for unramified extensions, $h(\mathcal{O}_L^\times) = 1$ implies $h(L^\times) = [L:K]$; (3) unramified invariant maps extend to all extensions, proving local CFT.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(12) Why is the classical definition of class formations non-canonical, and how does the basepoint problem arise?
Hint
The absolute Galois group $\Gamma$ requires choosing an algebraic closure $\overline{k}$, making $\Gamma$ defined only up to non-unique inner automorphism; the Galois category is an étale/connected groupoid, not an intrinsically based group.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(13) How does one generate enough cyclic extensions to establish class formations when roots of unity are missing?
Hint
Adjoin roots of unity and apply Kummer theory, using the non-degeneracy of the Kummer pairing $K^\times / (K^\times)^n \times \mathrm{Gal}(K(\sqrt[n]{K})/K) \to \mu_n$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(14) What is the Weil group of a class formation and how does it resolve the canonicity issue?
Hint
The Weil group $W_{L/K}$ is the group extension $1 \to A^L \to W_{L/K} \to \mathrm{Gal}(L/K) \to 1$ classified by the fundamental class $\alpha \in H^2(\mathrm{Gal}(L/K), A^L)$; Clausen refines this into an abelian gerbe on $B\Gamma$ banded by $A$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(15) How are cocycle classes and 2-morphisms interpreted at the chain level for gerbes?
Hint
A 2-cocycle is $x \in C^2$ with $dx = 0$ representing the extension class; a 1-cochain $\alpha \in C^1$ with $d\alpha = y - x$ defines a 1-isomorphism (2-morphism of extensions) between cocycles $x$ and $y$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(16) How are isomorphism classes of gerbes defined using 2-groupoids?
Hint
The 2-category of groupoids forms a $(2, 1)$-category where gerbes banded by $A$ over a site $\mathcal{C}$ are classified by $\pi_0 \mathrm{Map}(\mathcal{C}, B^2 A) \cong H^2(\mathcal{C}, A)$, with 1-morphisms being $A$-torsor equivalences and 2-morphisms being $A$-translations.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(17) What are the objects, 1-morphisms, and 2-morphisms in the categorical presentation of the Weil group?
Hint
Objects are inverse systems of group extensions $1 \to A^N \to E_N \to H/N \to 1$; 1-morphisms are morphisms of inverse systems compatible with projection to $H/N$; 2-morphisms are conjugations by elements of the abelian kernel $A^N$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(18) What is a refined class formation in the sense of Clausen/Scholze?
Hint
A triple $(\mathcal{C}, F, \alpha)$ where $\mathcal{C}$ is a Galois category, $F \colon \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}(\mathbb{Z})$ is a cosheaf valued in the derived $\infty$-category of condensed/discrete abelian groups such that $H_i(F(X)) = 0$ for $i \neq 0, 1$, and $\alpha \colon H_0(F(X)) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb{Z}$ is an isomorphism for every connected object $X \in \mathcal{C}$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(19) How does one promote a classical class formation to a refined class formation?
Hint
Construct a map $\kappa \colon \mathbb{Z}/\#\mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{R}\Gamma(\mathcal{C}, A)[2]$ in $\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{Z})$—where $\mathbb{Z}/\#\mathcal{C} = \bigcup_{X} \frac{1}{|X|}\mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Q}$—such that $\kappa$ induces an isomorphism $(\mathbb{Z}/\#\mathcal{C})/\mathbb{Z} \xrightarrow{\sim} H^2(\mathcal{C}, A)$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(20) What are the homotopy groups $\pi_0, \pi_1, \pi_2$ of the mapping space classifying promotions to refined class formations?
Hint
$\pi_0$ is the set of compatible fundamental classes in $\mathrm{Hom}((\mathbb{Z}/\#\mathcal{C})/\mathbb{Z}, H^2(\mathcal{C}, A))$; $\pi_1$ is the torsor under $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/\#\mathcal{C}, A(*))$; $\pi_2$ is $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/\#\mathcal{C}, A(*))$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(21) Why must $F$ be defined as a cosheaf, and how does this relate to its transpose $F^{\mathrm{tr}}$?
Hint
The homology invariant $H_1(F(X)) = A(X)$ assigns to a Galois cover its units/class group via pushforwards/norms, so $F$ is covariant on $\mathcal{C}$ (a cosheaf); its linear dual/transpose $F^{\mathrm{tr}} = \mathbf{R}\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(F, \mathbb{Z})$ is a contravariant sheaf on $\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(22) How does the refined class formation work for the base field $\mathbb{Q}$?
Hint
$H^2(G_\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q}^\times / \mathbb{Q}^\times) \cong \mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ has two choices of sign (homology/geometric Frobenius vs. cohomology/arithmetic Frobenius); $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q}^\times / \mathbb{Q}^\times) = 0$, and $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q}^\times / \mathbb{Q}^\times) \cong \mathbb{R}_{>0}^\times$, which contracts upon passing to norm-1 idèles, giving a canonical refined class formation.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(23) How does one obtain canonical refined class formations for general number fields from $\mathbb{Q}$?
Hint
By restricting the canonical refined class formation of $\mathbb{Q}$ along the finite étale slice $\mathcal{C}_K \subset \mathcal{C}_\mathbb{Q}$; the lift is unique up to an isomorphism that is unique up to powers of Frobenius.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(24) How are refined class formations constructed for finite fields and nonarchimedean local fields?
Hint
For $k = \mathbb{F}_q$ or a nonarchimedean local field $K$, $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/\#\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{O}_K^\times) \cong \widehat{\mathbb{Z}}/\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathrm{Hom} = 0$; fixing the canonical Frobenius generator gives a canonical lift to a refined class formation.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(25) How does one handle archimedean local fields $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{C}$ in refined class formations?
Hint
For $\mathbb{R}$, the Galois group is $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$; $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{R}^\times) = 0$ and $\mathrm{Hom}(\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{R}^\times) \cong \mathbb{R}^\times / \{\pm 1\} \cong \mathbb{R}_{>0}^\times$, which is canonically trivialized by taking positive norms.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(26) How do operations on refined class formations behave under base change?
Hint
Under a morphism of sites/Galois categories $f \colon \mathcal{C}' \to \mathcal{C}$, the pullback of a refined class formation is obtained by derived pushforward of the cosheaf $f_* F$, preserving the axioms.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(27) How does one define class field theory universally for locally compact Hausdorff number rings $R$?
Hint
Define an $\infty$-functor $F^{\mathrm{univ}}$ on the finite étale site of $R$ with $H_0(F^{\mathrm{univ}}(R)) = \mathbb{Z}$ and $H_1(F^{\mathrm{univ}}(R)) = C(R)$, the topological class group of $R$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(28) What are the classical class groups recovered by $H_1(F^{\mathrm{univ}}(R))$ across different rings $R$?
Hint
(1) Local field: $K^\times$; (2) Local ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$: $\mathcal{O}_K^\times$; (3) Finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$: $\mathbb{Z}$; (4) Global ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$: $\mathrm{Pic}(\mathcal{O}_K)$; (5) Global field $K$: idèle class group $C_K = \mathbb{A}_K^\times / K^\times$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(29) How does $K$-theory of locally compact modules universally produce class field theory?
Hint
The condensed $K$-theory spectrum $K(\mathbf{LCA}_R)$ of locally compact $R$-modules satisfies $K_1(\mathbf{LCA}_R) \cong C(R)$ (the class group), while $K_0(\mathbf{LCA}_R)$ contains topological dimension data that can be normalized to $\mathbb{Z}$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(30) How does the refined class formation assemble into the global Weil groupoid $\mathcal{W}$?
Hint
The gerbes over finite Galois quotients form an inverse system of topological 2-groupoids indexed by finite étale covers; taking the 2-limit $\mathcal{W} = \varprojlim_N E_N$ yields the Weil groupoid, whose connectedness ($\pi_0 \mathcal{W} = *$) follows from the compactness of the idèle class groups.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950

foundations of categorical measures
What is the primary objective of Jamneshan and Tao's framework for uncountable measure theory?
Hint
To develop measure theory, functional analysis, and ergodic theory without countability, separability, metrizability, or standard Borel/Lebesgue hypotheses, using category-theoretic dualities and canonical models.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.00681
foundations of categorical measures
How does the Gelfand duality operate between compact Hausdorff spaces and commutative C*-algebras?
Hint
The functor $C \colon \mathbf{CH} \to \mathbf{uCC^*Alg}^{\mathrm{op}}$ sending $X \mapsto C(X)$ is an equivalence of categories, with quasi-inverse spectrum functor $\mathrm{Spec} \colon \mathbf{uCC^*Alg}^{\mathrm{op}} \to \mathbf{CH}$ sending $A \mapsto \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{uCC^*Alg}}(A, \mathbb{C})$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.00681
foundations of categorical measures
How is Gelfand duality extended to locally compact Hausdorff (LCH) spaces and non-unital C*-algebras?
Hint
The functor $C_0 \colon \mathbf{LCH}_p \to \mathbf{CC^*Alg}_{nd}^{\mathrm{op}}$ (proper continuous maps and non-degenerate $*$-homomorphisms) is an equivalence; for non-proper continuous maps, morphisms map into the multiplier algebra $M(A)$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.00681
foundations of categorical measures
What are the minimal and maximal compactifications of an LCH space in this categorical framework?
Hint
The Alexandroff one-point compactification $X^+$ is the minimal compactification corresponding to the unitization $A^+ = C_0(X) \oplus \mathbb{C}$, while the Stone-Čech compactification $\beta X$ is the maximal compactification corresponding to the multiplier algebra $M(C_0(X)) = C_b(X)$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.00681
foundations of categorical measures
Why does uncountable measure theory adopt a Baire-centric rather than Borel-centric philosophy?
Hint
In non-metrizable spaces, the Borel $\sigma$-algebra is too large and points/compact sets may fail to be $G_\delta$; the Baire $\sigma$-algebras $C_0\text{-}\mathrm{Baire}(X)$ and $C_b\text{-}\mathrm{Baire}(X)$ are generated by continuous functions and interact naturally with functional analysis.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.00681
foundations of categorical measures
How is a Radon probability measure defined via inner regularity on an LCH space?
Hint
A probability measure $\mu$ on $C_0\text{-}\mathrm{Baire}(X)$ or $\mathrm{Borel}(X)$ is Radon if it is inner regular with respect to compact $G_\delta$ sets, meaning $\mu(E) = \sup \{ \mu(K) : K \subset E, K \text{ compact } G_\delta \}$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.00681
foundations of categorical measures
What is $\tau$-additivity ($\tau$-smoothness) and why does it eliminate pathological measure behavior?
Hint
A measure $\mu$ is $\tau$-additive if $\mu(\bigcup U_\alpha) = \sup \mu(U_\alpha)$ for every upward-directed net of open sets; on Baire sets, $\tau$-smoothness corresponds to $\lim \lambda(f_\alpha) = 0$ for decreasing nets $f_\alpha \downarrow 0$, making Radon hypotheses automatic on compact spaces.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.00681
foundations of categorical measures
How do Riesz dualities augment Gelfand dualities in the presence of measures and traces?
Hint
The Riesz representation theorem establishes an equivalence between categories of compact/LCH probability spaces $(\mathbf{CHPrb}, \mathbf{LCHPrb})$ with Radon measures and categories of tracial commutative $C^*$-algebras $(\mathbf{uCC^*Alg}^\tau, \mathbf{CC^*Alg}^\tau)$ equipped with faithful positive states/traces.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.00681
foundations of categorical measures
What is an abstract probability algebra and what is the abstraction functor?
Hint
A probability algebra is a pair $(\mathcal{B}, \mu)$ where $\mathcal{B}$ is a Dedekind $\sigma$-complete Boolean algebra and $\mu$ is a strictly positive, countably additive measure; the abstraction functor $\mathbf{Alg} \colon \mathbf{CncPrb} \to \mathbf{PrbAlg}$ quotients out the ideal of null sets $\Sigma_X / \mathcal{N}_\mu$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.00681
foundations of categorical measures
How is the category of probability algebras dual to commutative tracial von Neumann algebras?
Hint
By probability duality, $\mathbf{PrbAlg}$ is equivalent to $(\mathbf{CvNAlg}^\tau)^{\mathrm{op}}$ via the functor assigning $(\mathcal{B}, \mu)$ to its $L^\infty(\mathcal{B}, \mu)$ space equipped with the integral trace $\tau(f) = \int f\, d\mu$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.00681
foundations of categorical measures
What is the canonical model functor $\mathtt{Conc} \colon \mathbf{PrbAlg} \to \mathbf{CHPrb}$?
Hint
Defined by $\mathtt{Conc}(X) := \mathtt{Riesz}(L^\infty(X)_{\mathbf{uCC^*Alg}^\tau}) = \mathrm{Spec}(L^\infty(X))$; it assigns to every abstract probability algebra $X$ an extremally disconnected compact Hausdorff Stone probability space modeling $X$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.00681
foundations of categorical measures
What universal properties does the canonical model $\mathtt{Conc}(X)$ satisfy?
Hint
$\mathtt{Conc}(X)$ is an extremally disconnected Stone space satisfying the strong Lusin property (every bounded Baire-measurable function equals a unique continuous function almost everywhere) and acts as a universal concrete representative for $X$ analogous to the Stone-Čech compactification.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.00681
foundations of categorical measures
How does the canonical model provide canonical disintegration of probability measures?
Hint
Given a morphism of probability algebras $T \colon Y \to X$, the functoriality of $\mathtt{Conc}$ induces a unique continuous measure-preserving map $\pi \colon \mathtt{Conc}(X) \to \mathtt{Conc}(Y)$ whose fiber measures $y \mapsto \mu_y$ provide a canonical, point-everywhere defined disintegration without exceptional null sets.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.00681
foundations of categorical measures
How does the Loomis-Sikorski theorem realize abstract $\sigma$-algebras as concrete quotients?
Hint
The Loomis-Sikorski functor $\mathtt{LS} = \mathtt{Meager} \circ \mathtt{Stone}$ represents any abstract $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{B}$ as the concrete quotient $\mathrm{Baire}(S(\mathcal{B})) / \mathcal{M}$, where $S(\mathcal{B})$ is the Stone space and $\mathcal{M}$ is the $\sigma$-ideal of meager Baire sets.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.00681
foundations of categorical measures
How does the Loomis-Sikorski theorem yield an abstract Kolmogorov Extension Theorem?
Hint
Combining Stone duality with the Riesz representation theorem on product Stone spaces allows projective systems of probability algebras to admit projective limits without requiring Polish or topological regularity assumptions.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.00681
foundations of categorical measures
How does the Baire Category Theorem provide a qualitative analogue of measure theory?
Hint
BCT implies that in LCH or completely metrizable spaces, meager sets (countable unions of nowhere dense sets) model "negligible/null sets" and comeager sets model "full measure sets", preserving the intuition that countable intersections of dense open sets remain dense.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.00681
Gallauer
How did Emmy Noether conceptualize Betti numbers in the development of homology?
Hint
Noether showed that Betti numbers are numeric shadows of the underlying homology groups $H_n(X)$, which are abelian groups measuring the difference between closed cycles and exact boundaries; homology is a strictly richer algebraic invariant that cannot be recovered from Betti numbers alone.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
How does the Weil zeta function of a variety over a finite field motivate cohomology theories in arithmetic geometry?
Hint
The zeta function $\zeta_X(T) = \exp\left(\sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{\#X(\mathbb{F}_{q^n})}{n} T^n\right)$ packages point counts over all finite extensions; Weil's proof for curves and his conjectures for higher-dimensional varieties predicted that $\zeta_X(T)$ is a rational function whose zeroes and poles are governed by a well-behaved Weil cohomology theory ($\ell$-adic étale cohomology).
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
What is the categorification principle from numbers to abelian groups and cohomology?
Hint
While numbers have few interesting maps between them, abelian groups and chain complexes possess rich morphism spaces and derived invariants; passing from numbers to derived categories of sheaves categorifies numerical invariants into six-functor formalisms.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
Why does Grothendieck's relative point of view require the six operations?
Hint
Rather than studying isolated varieties $X$, one studies families and morphisms $f \colon X \to Y$; on non-proper varieties, global invariants fail to behave well without compactly supported pushforwards $f_!$ and exceptional pullbacks $f^!$, completing the six operations $(f^*, f_*, f_!, f^!, \otimes, \underline{\mathrm{Hom}})$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
What are the classical sheaf operations and how does the exceptional pushforward $f_!$ relate to its right adjoint $f^!$?
Hint
$f^*$ (inverse image) and $f_*$ (direct image) form a standard adjoint pair; on locally compact Hausdorff spaces / schemes, $f_!$ (compactly supported pushforward) preserves colimits and admits a right adjoint $f^!$ (exceptional pullback/twist) only in the derived $\infty$-category setting.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
How are cohomology, compactly supported cohomology, Borel-Moore homology, and homology expressed in terms of the six operations on the tensor unit $\mathbf{1}$?
Hint
Let $p \colon X \to *$ be the structure map. (1) Cohomology: $C^*(X) = p_* p^*(\mathbf{1})$; (2) Compactly supported cohomology: $C_c^*(X) = p_! p^*(\mathbf{1})$; (3) Borel-Moore homology: $C_*^{\mathrm{BM}}(X) = p_* p^!(\mathbf{1})$; (4) Homology with compact supports: $C_*(X) = p_! p^!(\mathbf{1})$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
How does Verdier duality operate between these four theories via the dualizing object $\omega_X = p^!\mathbf{1}$?
Hint
The adjunctions induce a canonical pairing $\mathbf{R}\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(p_! p^* \mathbf{1}, \mathbf{1}) \simeq p_* \mathbf{R}\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(p^* \mathbf{1}, p^! \mathbf{1}) = p_* p^! \mathbf{1}$, identifying the dual of compactly supported cohomology $C_c^*(X)^\vee$ with Borel-Moore homology $C_*^{\mathrm{BM}}(X)$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
How do different geometric coefficient systems determine specific cohomology theories?
Hint
(1) Constructible $\ell$-adic sheaves $\mathcal{D}_c^b(X, \mathbb{Q}_\ell) \implies$ étale cohomology; (2) Constructible topological sheaves $\mathcal{D}_c^b(X^{\mathrm{an}}, \Lambda) \implies$ Betti cohomology; (3) Holonomic $\mathcal{D}$-modules $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{hol}}^b(\mathcal{D}_X) \implies$ algebraic de Rham cohomology; (4) Voevodsky motives $\mathcal{DM}(X) \implies$ motivic cohomology.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
How are vanishing/nearby cycle functors, Chern classes, and regulator maps viewed in the six-functor context?
Hint
Nearby/vanishing cycles are specialized gluing functors across degenerations; Chern classes and cycle/regulator maps are natural transformations between different six-functor coefficient systems (e.g., from motivic cohomology to étale or de Rham cohomology).
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
What does proper pushforward mean for the transformation $f_! \to f_*$?
Hint
The canonical "forget supports" natural transformation $\alpha_f \colon f_! \to f_*$ is an isomorphism if and only if $f$ is proper.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
How does Grothendieck duality specialize to Poincaré and Serre dualities?
Hint
For a smooth morphism $f \colon X \to *$, relative purity computes $f^!\mathbf{1} \simeq \mathbf{1}(d)[2d]$; for $\ell$-adic coefficients, this yields $H^n(X, \mathbb{Q}_\ell)^\vee \cong H_c^{2d-n}(X, \mathbb{Q}_\ell(d))$ (Poincaré duality), and for coherent sheaves on proper $X$, it yields $\mathrm{Ext}^i(\mathcal{F}, \omega_X) \cong H^{n-i}(X, \mathcal{F})^\vee$ (Serre duality).
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
What is the proper projection formula and what does it assert?
Hint
For any morphism $f \colon X \to Y$, there is a natural isomorphism $f_!(A \otimes^{\mathbf{L}} f^*B) \xrightarrow{\sim} f_!(A) \otimes^{\mathbf{L}} B$, asserting that $f_!$ is an enriched $\mathcal{D}(Y)$-linear module functor.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
What is relative purity and how is it measured by the relative dualizing object?
Hint
For a smooth morphism $f$ of relative dimension $d$, relative purity is the natural equivalence $f^!(-) \simeq f^*(-) \otimes f^!(\mathbf{1}) \simeq f^*(-)(d)[2d]$, identifying $f^!$ as a Tate-twisted shift of $f^*$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456

How do open covers give rise to Mayer-Vietoris exact triangles in six-functor formalisms?
Hint
For an open cover $X = U \cup V$ with intersection $W = U \cap V$, the localization sequences for open immersions glue to produce the distinguished triangle $C^*(X) \to C^*(U) \oplus C^*(V) \to C^*(W) \xrightarrow{+1}$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456

Gallauer

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
How does the abstract blow-up square encode blow-up excision in cohomology via proper base change?
Hint
For a blow-up $\widetilde{X} \to X$ with center $Z$ and exceptional divisor $E$, the Cartesian square is an abstract cdh-distinguished square; proper base change and localization formally produce the excision fiber sequence $C^*(X) \to C^*(\widetilde{X}) \oplus C^*(Z) \to C^*(E) \xrightarrow{+1}$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
What is the Beck-Chevalley condition for a Cartesian square?
Hint
For a Cartesian square with projections $f, g, f', g'$, the natural transformation $g^* f_* \to f'_* g'^*$ (or $g^* f_! \to f'_! g'^*$) formed by adjunction units and counits is an isomorphism.

Gallauer
What is proper base change vs. smooth base change?
Hint
Proper base change states $g^* f_* \xrightarrow{\sim} f'_* g'^*$ when $f$ is proper; smooth base change states $g'_! f'^! \xrightarrow{\sim} f^! g_!$ (and $g^* f_* \xrightarrow{\sim} f'_* g'^*$) when $g$ is smooth.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
Why does the pullback along a smooth morphism admit a left adjoint $p_\#$?
Hint
By relative purity, $p^*(-) \simeq p^!(-)(-d)[-2d]$; since $p^!$ is right adjoint to $p_!$, $p^*$ admits the left adjoint $p_\#(-) := p_!(-)(d)[2d]$.

Gallauer
What is a Nisnevich-Mayer-Vietoris square?
Hint
An elementary distinguished square where $U \hookrightarrow X$ is an open immersion, $V \to X$ is an étale morphism, and $(V \setminus V \times_X U) \to (X \setminus U)$ is an isomorphism; coefficient systems satisfy descent on these squares.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer

A functor $\mathcal{D} \colon \mathbf{Sch}_S^{\mathrm{op}} \to \mathbf{CAlg}(\mathbf{Pr}_{\mathrm{st}}^{\mathrm{L}})$ assigning presentable stable symmetric monoidal $\infty$-categories satisfying: (1) smooth base change; (2) smooth projection formula; (3) localization; (4) $\mathbb{A}^1$-homotopy invariance; and (5) Tate stability ($\mathbf{1}(1)$ is $\otimes$-invertible).

Gallauer

Any coefficient system $\mathcal{D}$ uniquely extends to a full six-functor formalism equipped with $(f^*, f_*, f_!, f^!, \otimes, \underline{\mathrm{Hom}})$, Grothendieck duality, proper base change, and the projection formula; morphisms of coefficient systems induce morphisms of six-functor formalisms.

Gallauer
How did Voevodsky establish that exceptional functoriality $f_!$ arises from localization and $\mathbb{A}^1$-homotopy?
Hint
Voevodsky proved that compactifications and purity formulas can be reconstructed purely from the localization sequences of open/closed immersions combined with $\mathbb{A}^1$-invariance, defining $f_!$ as a localized homotopy pushforward without manual compactifications.

Why does cohomology possess a ring structure (cup product) while homology possesses a coalgebra structure?

What are the homotopy groups of the $\ell$-adic completed $K$-theory of a strictly Henselian local ring $R$ (with $\ell \in R^\times$)?
Hint
Gabber-Suslin rigidity shows $\pi_i K(R)_{\ell}^\wedge \cong \pi_i K(k)_{\ell}^\wedge \cong \mathbb{Z}_\ell(j)$ for $i = 2j$ even, and $0$ for $i$ odd (matching topological complex $K$-theory).
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.26269
Scholze's six functor formalisms (mini)
What is the local-to-global spectral sequence relating étale cohomology to $\ell$-adic $K$-theory?
Hint
The Quillen-Lichtenbaum / motivic spectral sequence $E_2^{p, q} = H^{p-q}(X_{\text{ét}}, \mathbb{Z}_\ell(-q)) \implies \pi_{-(p+q)} K(X)_{\ell}^\wedge$ for $p \le q \le 0$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.26269
Scholze's six functor formalisms (mini)
How is a six-functor formalism encoded as a lax symmetric monoidal functor on correspondences?
Hint
As a lax symmetric monoidal $\infty$-functor $\mathcal{D} \colon \mathrm{Corr}(\mathcal{C}, E) \to \mathbf{Cat}_\infty$, where 1-morphisms encode $(g^*, f_!)$, right adjoints produce $f^!$ and $g_*$, and monoidality encodes the projection formula and Künneth isomorphisms.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.26269
Scholze's six functor formalisms (mini)
How do Grothendieck's Cartesian fibrations and Lurie's straightening/unstraightening equivalence work?
Hint
The straightening/unstraightening theorem provides an equivalence of $\infty$-categories between Cartesian/coCartesian fibrations over $\mathcal{C}$ and functors $\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}} \to \mathbf{Cat}_\infty$ (resp. $\mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Cat}_\infty$).
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.26269
Scholze's six functor formalisms (mini)
How is a symmetric monoidal $\infty$-category defined via coCartesian fibrations over $\mathbf{Fin}_*$?
Hint
As a coCartesian fibration $C^\otimes \to \mathbf{Fin}_*$ such that for every finite pointed set $\langle n \rangle$, the induced maps $\rho^i \colon \langle n \rangle \to \langle 1 \rangle$ induce an equivalence $C_{\langle n \rangle}^\otimes \xrightarrow{\sim} (C_{\langle 1 \rangle}^\otimes)^n$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.26269
Scholze's six functor formalisms (mini)
How does the combinatorics of correspondences automatically produce the projection formula?
Hint
The composition of the diagonal correspondence and the product correspondence in $\mathrm{Corr}(\mathcal{C}, E)$ yields $f_!(A \otimes f^*B) \cong f_!(A) \otimes B$ as a formal consequence of functoriality.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.26269
Scholze's six functor formalisms (mini)
What are the minimal geometric axioms on $(I, P)$ needed to construct a six-functor formalism?
Hint
$I$ (open immersions) and $P$ (proper maps) must be stable under compositions, base change, and diagonals, satisfy $I \cap P = \mathrm{Isom}$, and ensure every $f \in E$ factors as $f = p \circ j$ with $j \in I$ and $p \in P$ (Nagata compactification).
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.26269
Scholze's six functor formalisms (mini)
What is the definition of cohomological smoothness for a morphism $f \colon X \to Y$?
Hint
A morphism $f$ is cohomologically smooth if $f_!$ admits a right adjoint $f^!$, the relative dualizing object $\omega_{f} := f^!(\mathbf{1}_Y)$ is $\otimes$-invertible in $\mathcal{D}(X)$, and the canonical map $f^*(-) \otimes \omega_f \xrightarrow{\sim} f^!(-)$ is an isomorphism compatible with arbitrary base change.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.26269
Scholze's six functor formalisms (mini)
Why is cohomological smoothness more general than classical geometric smoothness?
Hint
Because it is defined purely through the existence of Poincaré-Verdier duality and invertible dualizing sheaves, holding for rigid analytic and perfectoid spaces without requiring smooth charts.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.26269
Page 6 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
How does one characterize the sheaf of holomorphic functions locally and globally on complex domains?
Hint
A holomorphic function is locally given on open polydiscs by power series converging absolutely and uniformly; since holomorphicity is local, it glues to a sheaf $\mathcal{O}_X$ whose higher sheaf cohomology vanishes on Stein domains by Cartan's Theorem B.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 7 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
How does one establish the existence and cohomological vanishing of the sheaf of holomorphic functions?
Hint
Analyticity follows from the Cauchy integral formula; using smooth bump functions and partitions of unity, one constructs the Dolbeault resolution $0 \to \mathcal{O} \to \Omega^{0,0} \xrightarrow{\bar{\partial}} \Omega^{0,1} \xrightarrow{\bar{\partial}} \dots$, reducing higher cohomology vanishing to the solvability of the $\bar{\partial}$-equation on Stein/polydisc domains.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 8 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
What is the motivating idea behind an analytic ring structure on a topological ring?
Hint
An analytic ring structure specifies a functorial topological module of "measures" $\mathcal{M}(S)$ for every profinite set $S$, enabling a unique integration/extension map from functions on $S$ to summable series and integrals in the module category.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 8 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
Why is the one-point compactification $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ relevant as a test space?
Hint
$\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ is a countable cofiltered limit of finite discrete sets (hence profinite), serving as the universal test space for convergent sequences and summability.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 8 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
Why does the naive topological module of Radon measures fail over $\mathbb{R}$?
Hint
The space of Radon measures on a profinite set is not complete under general algebraic operations and lacks good categorical exactness properties because topological abelian groups do not form an abelian category.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 8 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
Why do topological abelian groups fail to form an abelian category?
Hint
A continuous bijective homomorphism between topological abelian groups (e.g., from discrete $\mathbb{R}$ to standard $\mathbb{R}$) has trivial kernel and cokernel but is not an open isomorphism, so the First Isomorphism Theorem fails.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 9 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
How does condensed mathematics resolve the failure of the First Isomorphism Theorem for topological groups?
Hint
By embedding topological groups into condensed abelian groups via their functor of points on profinite sets; the quotient of standard $\mathbb{R}$ by discrete $\mathbb{R}$ becomes a non-trivial condensed abelian group sheaf.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 10 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
What is the rigorous preliminary definition of an analytic ring?
Hint
An analytic ring is a condensed ring $\mathcal{A}$ equipped with a family of condensed $\mathcal{A}$-modules $\mathcal{M}(S)$ of "measures" for profinite sets $S$, together with Dirac-delta maps $S \to \mathcal{M}(S)$ such that the category of $\mathcal{M}$-complete $\mathcal{A}$-modules forms an abelian subcategory/heart of $\mathbf{Cond}(\mathcal{A})$ stable under limits, colimits, and extensions.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 11 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
Why promote the classical sheaf of holomorphic functions to an abelian tensor category?
Hint
To obtain a category of modules with well-behaved completed tensor products and homological algebra (derived categories) that unifies functional analysis with algebraic geometry.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 11 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
How are profinite sets characterized as a cofiltered limit of finite sets?
Hint
Every compact Hausdorff totally disconnected space $S$ is canonically isomorphic to $\varprojlim_{i} S_i$, where $S_i$ runs over all finite partitions of $S$ into clopen subsets ordered by refinement.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 11 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
What is the finitary Grothendieck topology on the category of $\kappa$-small profinite sets $\mathbf{Prof}_\kappa$?
Hint
A covering of a profinite set $S$ is a finite family of continuous maps $\{f_i \colon S_i \to S\}$ such that the induced map $\coprod_{i=1}^n S_i \to S$ is surjective.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 12 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
What is the category of $\kappa$-condensed sets and how does it behave under cardinal cutoffs?
Hint
$\mathbf{Cond}_\kappa(\mathbf{Set})$ is the category of sheaves on $(\mathbf{Prof}_\kappa, \text{finitary étale})$, i.e., contravariant functors $X \colon \mathbf{Prof}_\kappa^{\mathrm{op}} \to \mathbf{Set}$ sending finite coproducts to finite products and preserving covers; taking the colimit over strong limit cardinals $\kappa$ yields the fully faithful category $\mathbf{Cond}(\mathbf{Set})$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 13 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
What is a quasi-compact condensed set?
Hint
A condensed set $X$ such that for every collection of open coverings, any covering surjection $\coprod_{i} U_i \to X$ admits a finite sub-surjection; equivalently, $X$ admits a surjection from a single profinite set.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 13 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
Why is a condensed set quasi-compact if and only if it is a quotient of a profinite set?
Hint
Profinite sets are quasi-compact projective generators; every condensed set is a canonical colimit of profinite sets, so finite subcoverings correspond precisely to surjections $S \twoheadrightarrow X$ from a profinite set $S$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 13 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
What is a quasi-separated condensed set?
Hint
A condensed set $X$ whose diagonal morphism $\Delta \colon X \to X \times X$ is quasi-compact, meaning for any two maps from profinite sets $S, T \to X$, the fiber product $S \times_X T$ is quasi-compact.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 13 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
How are compact Hausdorff spaces embedded into condensed sets?
Hint
The subcategory of quasi-compact quasi-separated (qcqs) condensed sets is equivalent to the category of compact Hausdorff topological spaces via $X \mapsto \underline{X}(S) = C(S, X)$, representing closed equivalence relations on profinite sets.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 14 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
What does it mean for a condensed set $X$ to be projective?
Hint
For every surjective map of condensed sets $Y \twoheadrightarrow Z$, the induced map $\mathrm{Hom}(X, Y) \to \mathrm{Hom}(X, Z)$ is surjective; equivalently, any surjection $Y \twoheadrightarrow X$ admits a section.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 14 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
Why does the Stone-Čech compactification $\beta I$ serve as a projective generator for condensed sets?
Hint
For any discrete set $I$, the Stone-Čech compactification $\beta I$ is an extremally disconnected profinite set, and Gleason's theorem implies $\beta I$ is a projective object in the category of compact Hausdorff spaces and condensed sets.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 15 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
Why does the category of condensed abelian groups $\mathbf{Cond}(\mathbf{Ab})$ possess good homological properties?
Hint
$\mathbf{Cond}(\mathbf{Ab})$ is a Grothendieck abelian category with enough compact projective objects given by the free condensed abelian groups $\mathbb{Z}[S]$ for extremally disconnected profinite sets $S$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 15 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
Why is $\mathbb{Z}[S]$ compact projective for an extremally disconnected profinite set $S$?
Hint
The functor $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Cond}(\mathbf{Ab})}(\mathbb{Z}[S], -) \cong \underline{(-)}(S)$ preserves all colimits and all exact sequences because $S$ is extremally disconnected and compact.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 16 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
What is the concept of a liquid vector space over $\mathbb{R}$? (Hint: A condensed $\mathbb{R}$-vector space $V$ that is complete with respect to $p$-summable measures, meaning for every $p \in (0, 1]$, infinite sums of $p$-convex combinations converge uniquely in $V$.)
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 16 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
How are signed Radon measures with bounded $p$-variation defined algebraically on profinite sets?
Hint
For a profinite set $S = \varprojlim S_i$, the condensed module of $p$-measures is $\mathcal{M}_{\le p}(S) = \bigcup_{C > 0} \varprojlim_{i} \{ (a_s) \in \mathbb{R}[S_i] : \sum |a_s|^p \le C \}$, forming the unit balls of $\ell^p(S)$ under non-convex $p$-norms.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 18 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
What is the condensed ring module of $p$-Radon measures $\mathcal{M}_{<p}(S)$?
Hint
$\mathcal{M}_{<p}(S) := \varinjlim_{p' < p} \mathcal{M}_{\le p'}(S)$, defined as the filtered colimit of bounded $\ell^{p'}$-variation measure balls to ensure exactness and monoidal properties.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 19 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
State the fundamental definition of a $p$-liquid vector space
Hint
A condensed abelian group $V$ is $p$-liquid if for every profinite set $S$, the natural evaluation map $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Cond}(\mathbf{Ab})}(\mathcal{M}_{<p}(S), V) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathrm{Map}(S, V)$ is an isomorphism of condensed abelian groups.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 19 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
Why are $p$-Banach spaces and their inverse limits $p$-liquid?
Hint
A $p$-Banach space $(B, \|\cdot\|)$ is sequentially complete under its $p$-norm ($\|x+y\| \le \|x\| + \|y\|$), ensuring all series with $\sum \|x_n\|^p < \infty$ converge uniquely, which matches the integration axiom against $\mathcal{M}_{<p}(S)$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 20 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
Why is $\mathcal{M}_{<p}(S)$ not Banach, and how is its internal dual characterized?
Hint
$\mathcal{M}_{<p}(S)$ is a strict inductive limit of non-convex metric spaces; its internal continuous dual is $\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathcal{M}_{<p}(S), \mathbb{R}) \cong C(S, \mathbb{R})$, recovering the classical Banach space of continuous real functions on $S$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 22 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
How is a condensed set characterized via extremally disconnected test spaces?
Hint
A condensed set is uniquely determined as a contravariant functor from the category of extremally disconnected profinite sets $\mathbf{ExtrProf}^{\mathrm{op}}$ to $\mathbf{Set}$ that preserves finite products.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 22 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
What is the algebraic duality between profinite sets and Boolean algebras?
Hint
Stone duality: $\mathbf{Prof}^{\mathrm{op}} \simeq \mathbf{Bool}$ (Boolean algebras via clopen subsets) and $\mathbf{ExtrProf}^{\mathrm{op}} \simeq \mathbf{CBool}$ (complete Boolean algebras).

Page 23 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
Why can the free condensed abelian group $\mathbb{Z}[S]$ be written as a countable union of profinite sets?
Hint
For $S$ profinite, $\mathbb{Z}[S] = \bigcup_{n \ge 1} (\sum_{i=1}^n \pm S)$, which is a countable union of compact Hausdorff/profinite subspaces inside the condensed group.

Page 24 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
When is a condensed abelian group flat?

$M \in \mathbf{Cond}(\mathbf{Ab})$ is flat if and only if for every extremally disconnected profinite set $S$, the evaluation $M(S)$ is a torsion-free discrete abelian group.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 25 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
How are compact projective condensed abelian groups characterized?
Hint
An object is compact projective in $\mathbf{Cond}(\mathbf{Ab})$ if and only if it is a retract of $\mathbb{Z}[\beta I]$ for some set $I$, where $\beta I$ is the Stone-Čech compactification of discrete $I$.

Page 26 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
Why are internal Ext groups non-zero in condensed mathematics?

Because $\mathbf{Cond}(\mathbf{Ab})$ contains topological data; for example, $\underline{\mathrm{Ext}}^1(\underline{\mathbb{R}}, \underline{\mathbb{Z}}) \cong \underline{\mathbb{R}}/\underline{\mathbb{Z}} \cong \mathbb{S}^1 \neq 0$, capturing non-trivial extensions of topological groups.

Page 26 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
Why is the projective tensor product $\mathbb{Z}[\beta I] \otimes \mathbb{Z}[\beta J]$ not projective?

Page 27 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
State Theorem 3.11 on the structure of the category $\mathbf{Liq}_p$ of $p$-liquid vector spaces
Hint
$\mathbf{Liq}_p$ is an abelian subcategory of $\mathbf{Cond}(\mathbf{Ab})$ stable under all limits, colimits, extensions, and internal $\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}$ and $\underline{\mathrm{Ext}}$; the inclusion derived functor $\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{Liq}_p) \hookrightarrow \mathcal{D}(\mathbf{Cond}(\mathbf{Ab}))$ is fully faithful and admits a left adjoint $p$-liquification functor $(-)_{{\mathrm{liq}}_p}$ that is symmetric monoidal with unit $\mathbb{R}$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 35 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
What are gaseous and solid vector spaces over $\mathbb{Q}_p$?

Over nonarchimedean fields like $\mathbb{Q}_p$, the measures $\mathcal{M}(S) = \mathbb{Z}_p[[S]]$ produce the abelian category of solid vector spaces $\mathbf{Solid}_{\mathbb{Q}_p}$; intermediate growth rate conditions yield $p$-liquid / gaseous structures.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 38 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
How is the liquid tensor product defined?
Hint
The liquid tensor product $V \otimes_{\mathbf{Liq}_p}^{\mathbf{L}} W := (V \otimes_{\mathbf{Cond}(\mathbf{Ab})}^{\mathbf{L}} W)_{{\mathrm{liq}}_p}$ is the liquification of the condensed derived tensor product, completing it with respect to $p$-summable measures.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 40 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
How are $p$-measures defined on locally profinite topological spaces?

For a locally profinite space $X = \bigcup U_i$, a $p$-measure is a finitely additive measure of bounded $p$-variation on compact open subsets, forming a condensed $\mathbb{R}$-module $\mathcal{M}_{<p}(X) = \varinjlim_{K \subset X} \mathcal{M}_{<p}(K)$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 44 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
How does Poincaré duality motivate liquid analytic geometry?
Hint
Liquid modules allow the formulation of a six-operation formalism $(f^*, f_*, f_!, f^!, \otimes, \underline{\mathrm{Hom}})$ on non-archimedean and complex analytic spaces, realizing Poincaré and Serre duality via derived trace maps.

Page 48 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
What role does the one-point compactification play in functional analysis on liquid spaces?
Hint
It compactifies non-compact domains (like $\mathbb{C}$ or $\mathbb{R}$), transforming compactly supported smooth/analytic distributions into global sections on a compact base.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 50 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
How do nuclear spaces resolve the non-isomorphism of sequence spaces?
Hint
Nuclear spaces are projective/inductive limits of Hilbert spaces with trace-class transition maps; their tensor products are uniquely defined without completing differently under projective vs. injective topologies.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 52 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
What is a locale and how is it used in analytic geometry?
Hint
A locale is a lattice/point-free space formalizing the frame of open sets; it avoids point-set pathologies when taking fiber products and spectrum constructions in non-archimedean/complex geometry.

Page 52 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
What is the Berkovich spectrum $\mathcal{M}(A)$ in terms of locales?

Page 59 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
How is the categorified locale $S(C)$ defined for a symmetric monoidal category $C$?

Page 63 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
What is an analytic space viewed as a categorified locale?

Page 85 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
State the liquid GAGA theorem for proper complex schemes

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 90 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
How does the relation "Finite = Compact + Discrete" characterize coherent sheaves?

Page 95 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
What is a nuclear module in liquid complex geometry?

Page 98 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
What is a trace-class / nuclear morphism in a closed symmetric monoidal category?

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 100 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
What is a dual nuclear Fréchet (DNF) space?
Hint
A condensed vector space that is a sequential filtered colimit of Hilbert spaces $H_0 \to H_1 \to H_2 \to \dots$ along injective transition maps that are of $p$-Schatten class.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 101 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
What is a $p$-Schatten operator between Hilbert spaces?
Hint
A compact operator $T \colon H_1 \to H_2$ whose singular values $(\sigma_n)_{n \ge 0}$ satisfy $\sum_{n=0}^\infty \sigma_n^p < \infty$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 102 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
When is an object in a compactly generated stable $\infty$-category $C$ called discrete?
Hint
An object $M \in C$ is discrete if it lies in the essential image of the base change functor $\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{End}(1)) \to C$ generated by colimits and shifts of the unit object $\mathbf{1}$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 102 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
When is an object in $C$ a perfect complex?
Hint
An object $V \in C$ is a perfect complex if and only if it is both compact and discrete, i.e., in the thick subcategory generated by the unit object under finite colimits, shifts, and retracts.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 103 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
How are compact nuclear objects characterized via trace-class maps?

An object is compact and nuclear if and only if it is dualizable in the liquid category, which occurs precisely when it is a retract of the fiber/cone of $\mathrm{id} - f \colon V \to V$ for a nuclear operator $f$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 103 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
When is a liquid category Fredholm?
Hint
A category is Fredholm if every dualizable object is discrete, ensuring that index theorems and finite-dimensionality of cohomology hold.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 103 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
What is the precise definition of an affinoid algebra in liquid complex geometry?
Hint
A commutative algebra $A \in \mathbf{CAlg}(\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{Liq}_p))$ that is quasi-isomorphic to a quotient of the algebra of overconvergent power series $\mathbb{C}\{T_1, \dots, T_n\}^\dagger$ on a polydisc by a finitely generated ideal.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 105 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
State the global definition of a complex analytic space
Hint
A complex analytic space is a categorified locale $(X, \mathcal{C}_X)$ over $(* , \mathcal{D}(\mathbf{Liq}_p))$ that is locally isomorphic to the categorified spectrum $\mathrm{Spec}(A, \mathcal{M}_{<p})$ of an affinoid liquid algebra $A$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Page 111 Complex Geometry and Condensed Mathematics
How are open and closed immersions defined for liquid complex analytic spaces?
Hint
An open immersion is a local isomorphism of categorified locales corresponding to restriction to an open sublocale; a closed immersion is a morphism corresponding to a surjective quotient of structure sheaves $A \twoheadrightarrow A/I$ in $\mathbf{Liq}_p$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.11731
Slide 2 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
How did Newton historically introduce operator-theoretic ideas into mechanics?
Hint
By replacing static geometric variables with fluxions and differential operators acting on functions, anticipating the operational formalism of quantum observables.

Slide 5 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
Why does quantum mechanics provide a more subtle answer to the nature of space and the reduction of the wave packet?
Hint
The collapse of the wave packet is an irreversible thermodynamic phenomenon; observables are non-commuting operators on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$, meaning quantum states interact non-trivially with the algebra of observables.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 8 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
How does physical time emerge from quantum thermodynamics and thermal equilibrium?
Hint
A thermal equilibrium state at inverse temperature $\beta$ is given by the Gibbs state $\varphi(A) = \frac{\mathrm{Tr}(A e^{-\beta H})}{\mathrm{Tr}(e^{-\beta H})}$; time evolution $A \mapsto \sigma_t(A) = e^{i t H} A e^{-i t H}$ is uniquely determined by the algebraic KMS condition satisfied by $\varphi$.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 10 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
State the Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (KMS) condition at inverse temperature $\beta$
Hint
A faithful state $\varphi$ on a von Neumann algebra $M$ satisfies the $\mathrm{KMS}_\beta$ condition with respect to a 1-parameter automorphism group $\sigma_t$ if for all $x, y \in M$, there exists a bounded holomorphic function $F(z)$ on the strip $0 \le \mathrm{Im}(z) \le \beta$ such that $F(t) = \varphi(x \sigma_t(y))$ and $F(t + i\beta) = \varphi(\sigma_t(y) x)$.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 12 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
State the Tomita-Takesaki Theorem for von Neumann algebras
Hint
Let $M$ be a von Neumann algebra and $\varphi$ a faithful normal state on $M$. There exists a unique 1-parameter group of automorphisms $\sigma_t^\varphi \in \mathrm{Aut}(M)$ (the modular automorphism group) fulfilling the $\mathrm{KMS}_1$ condition with respect to $\varphi$.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 13 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
How did Connes' thesis establish that a von Neumann algebra possesses a canonical thermodynamic time evolution?
Hint
Connes proved the Radon-Nikodym cocycle theorem: for any two faithful normal states $\varphi, \psi$, the modular automorphism groups $\sigma_t^\varphi$ and $\sigma_t^\psi$ differ only by inner automorphisms $\mathrm{Ad}(u_t)$, yielding a canonical outer automorphism homomorphism $\delta \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathrm{Out}(M) = \mathrm{Aut}(M)/\mathrm{Inn}(M)$ independent of the state.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 15 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
How is time evolution interpreted algebraically in quantum gravity?
Hint
Time is not an external geometric parameter but the canonical 1-parameter group of outer automorphisms $\delta \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{M})$ of the non-commutative von Neumann algebra of gravitational observables.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 17 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
Why does the spectrum of the Laplacian fail to characterize a compact Riemannian manifold?
Hint
John Milnor constructed non-isometric 16-dimensional flat tori that are isospectral ($\mathrm{Spec}(\Delta_1) = \mathrm{Spec}(\Delta_2)$), proving that one cannot "hear the shape of a drum" from the eigenvalue spectrum alone.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 19 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
What missing operator-theoretic information is needed beyond the spectrum to reconstruct a manifold?
Hint
The relative position (commutation relations) of two abelian von Neumann algebras acting on the Hilbert space $L^2(M)$: the algebra of smooth coordinates $C^\infty(M)$ and the algebra of momentum operators/differential operators generated by the Dirac operator $D$.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 21 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
How does von Neumann's theorem characterize the algebra of bounded measurable functions on Hilbert space?
Hint
By von Neumann's uniqueness theorem, the maximal abelian $*$-algebra $L^\infty(M)$ acting by multiplication on $L^2(M)$ is uniquely isomorphic to the standard measure algebra of $M$, containing purely measure-theoretic, non-metric data.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 23 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
Why is the Dirac operator $D$ used instead of the scalar Laplacian $\Delta$?
Hint
The Dirac operator $D$ is a first-order differential operator providing a square root of the Laplacian ($D^2 = \Delta + \frac{1}{4}R$ via Lichnerowicz), whose inverse $D^{-1}$ represents the fermion propagator and directly encodes the metric and spin structure.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 25 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
What are the CKM invariant, $\mathrm{Spec}(D)$, and the relative spectrum $\mathrm{Spec}_N(M)$?
Hint
$\mathrm{Spec}(D)$ gives the energy levels/frequencies of the system, while the relative spectrum $\mathrm{Spec}_N(M)$ measures the relative modular position of $M$ inside $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$, encoding cross-correlations and transition probabilities between frequencies.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 27 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
How is the Riemannian geodesic distance defined spectrally in noncommutative geometry?
Hint
Connes' spectral distance formula replaces the infimum of arc lengths by the dual operator formula: $d(p, q) = \sup \{ |f(p) - f(q)| : f \in C^\infty(M), \|[D, f]\| \le 1 \}$, where the infinitesimal line element is $ds = D^{-1}$.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 29 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
How does noncommutative geometry describe spacetime unification in the Standard Model?
Hint
Spacetime is modeled as an almost-commutative spectral triple $(\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{H}, D)$ with algebra $\mathcal{A} = C^\infty(M) \otimes \mathcal{A}_F$, where $\mathcal{A}_F = \mathbb{C} \oplus \mathbb{H} \oplus M_3(\mathbb{C})$ corresponds to the finite non-commutative geometry of the Standard Model.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 31 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
Why is the group of inner automorphisms $\mathrm{Inn}(\mathcal{A})$ of $\mathcal{A} = C^\infty(M) \otimes M_n(\mathbb{C})$ identified with gauge transformations?
Hint
The automorphism group splits as a semi-direct product $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{A}) = \mathrm{Inn}(\mathcal{A}) \rtimes \mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{A})$, where $\mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{A}) \cong \mathrm{Diff}(M)$ gives gravity (diffeomorphisms) and $\mathrm{Inn}(\mathcal{A}) \cong C^\infty(M, \mathrm{SU}(n))$ gives the local internal gauge group.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 34 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
How does the shift from 4 to 10 dimensions arise in noncommutative geometry compared to string theory compactifications?
Hint
In string theory, 6 extra dimensions are compactified on an unnaturally small Calabi-Yau manifold; in NCG, the KO-dimension of the finite spectral triple $\mathcal{A}_F$ is $6 \pmod 8$, making the total metric/KO-dimension of spacetime $4 + 6 = 10 \equiv 2 \pmod 8$ without requiring geometric compactification.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 37 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
How does the Spectral Action Principle unify gravity with the Standard Model forces?
Hint
The full bosonic action is given by the spectral action $\mathrm{Tr}(f(D_A / \Lambda)) + \frac{1}{2}\langle J\psi, D_A \psi\rangle$, where $D_A = D + A + \epsilon J A J^{-1}$ is the Dirac operator with gauge fluctuations; its asymptotic heat kernel expansion automatically produces the Einstein-Hilbert action, the Yang-Mills gauge actions, and the Higgs potential with unified coupling relations at the unification scale $\Lambda$.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 4 primes
State Grothendieck's Galois-étale duality: the category of finite étale coverings of $X$ is equivalent to finite $\pi_1^{\text{ét}}(X, \bar{x})$-sets
https://ctta.igrothendieck.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Slides_ConnesAlain-1.pdf
Slide 9 primes
Explore the Mazur-Kapranov-Reznikov analogy between number fields and 3-manifolds: $\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})$ is analogous to $S^3$, primes $p$ correspond to knots $K_p \hookrightarrow S^3$, and $\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{F}_p)$ corresponds to the knot $S^1$
https://ctta.igrothendieck.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Slides_ConnesAlain-1.pdf
Slide 10 primes
Show that the étale fundamental group $\pi_1^{\text{ét}}(\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{Z}[1/p]))$ is analogous to the fundamental group of a knot complement $\pi_1(S^3 \setminus K_p)$, and the Legendre symbol corresponds to the linking number of knots
https://ctta.igrothendieck.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Slides_ConnesAlain-1.pdf
Slide 14 primes

How does one compute the partition function of a topological four-functor field theory?
Hint
A functor from the category of $d$-dimensional cobordisms; the partition function is the value of the functor on a $d$-torus, i.e. $Z(T)$. The partition function is the trace over the value of the QFT on the cylinder given by cutting, so the name comes from the cylinder cobordism of the manifold. On Riemannian cobordisms, the value of the QFT on a cylinder of length $t$ is a linear operator of the form $\exp(-\hbar)\, H$; here $H$ is the Hamiltonian (energy). What does one compute for a $0$-dimensional free QFT?
Hint
Take a positive definite symmetric matrix for simplicity, denoted $M$. Its inverse $M^{-1}$ is the propagator, and it appears in the action formula through the quadratic term $\frac12 M_{ab} \phi^{a}\phi^{b}$. The partition function is a Gaussian integral: $\int d^n\phi\, e^{-\frac{1}{2\hbar}\phi^{T}M\phi} = \frac{(2\pi\hbar)^{n/2}}{\sqrt{\det M}}$. Diagonalise $M$ (the action matrix), since the Lebesgue measure is invariant under an orthogonal map $O$, the integral factorises into $n$ independent $1$-dimensional Gaussian integrals over the eigenvectors; this reduces free QFT to classical probability theory.

What is Wick's probability theorem (Isserlis' theorem)?
Hint
For a zero-mean multivariate normal random vector $X_1,\dots X_{2k}$, the expectation $\mathbb{E}(X_1X_2\cdots X_{2k})$ is a sum over all complete pairings, each term a product of the $2k$ covariance entries, e.g. $\sum_{\text{pairings}}\prod_{(a,b)\text{pair}} \mathbb{E}(X_aX_b)$. How does one invent the notion of a sigma-algebra?
Hint
Need to eventually obtain the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, which is needed for uniqueness when containing a topology. A $\sigma$-algebra serves as the parameter space for a measure; visualize it as sets or "blobs" where the complement of a blob is in the $\sigma$-algebra, the empty set is in the $\sigma$-algebra, and arbitrary countable unions of blobs are in the $\sigma$-algebra. A measure is a map assigning a non-negative extended real number to each set in a $\sigma$-algebra such that the empty set has measure zero and countable unions of disjoint sets satisfy countable additivity $\mu(\bigcup E_i) = \sum \mu(E_i)$. Disjointness prevents overlap. The key mental image is blobs, complements of blobs, and countable unions.

How does one invent the integral with respect to a measure?

Given a measure space, assign non-negative measurable functions to integrals that are linear and satisfy the monotone convergence theorem, meaning if a monotone increasing sequence of functions converges pointwise, then their integrals converge to the integral of the limit. Lastly, integrating against an indicator function $\mathbf{1}_A$ recovers the measure $\mu(A)$. The key intuition is linear, non-interacting decomposition into a basis similar to Fourier analysis.

How does one invent and prove the dominated convergence theorem?

Let $f_n$ be a sequence in a measure space such that $f_n \to f$ almost everywhere. If there exists an integrable dominating function $g$ such that $|f_n| \le g$ almost everywhere, then $\lim \int f_n \, d\mu = \int f \, d\mu$. Prove this by applying Fatou's lemma to $g - f_n$ and $g + f_n$. The easiest intuition is a bounded envelope; domination acts as a compactness condition analogous to sequential weak compactness in $L^p$ spaces.

How does one prove the existence and uniqueness of conditional expectation?
Hint

Extend to non-negative $X \in \mathcal{m}\mathcal{E}_+$ using monotone convergence of $X \wedge n$ and indicator tests. Slide 9 class field theory in 33 slides
What is the geometry significance of Hilbert's Theorem 90 and what is the purpose of the first Galois cohomology?
Hint
vector spaces descend uniquely from the finite Galois extension $K$ to the field $k$, and there are no nontrivial $k$-forms of $K^n$. Note that this changes for other algebraic groups. For example, the projective linear group which classifies central simple algebras via the first Galois cohomology. The orthogonal group classifies the quadratic forms. The unitary group classifies the hermitian forms. Therefore, the first Galois cohomology is used to classify forms.
http://mat.msgsu.edu.tr/~aad/2012/Slides/paganin.pdf

Hint

Page 24 Blechschmidt's thesis and slides
Is finite coproduct $\mathcal{F} \amalg \mathcal{G}$ geometric?

Is arbitrary coproduct $\coprod_{i \in I} \mathcal{F}_i$ geometric?

Page 24 Blechschmidt's thesis and slides

Page 24 Blechschmidt's thesis and slides

Makkai Conceptual Completeness and Ultracategories by Jacob Lurie
(From Stone Duality to Conceptual Completeness) Review classical Stone duality for Boolean algebras: the contravariant functor $\operatorname{Spec}: \mathbf{Bool}^{\text{op}} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbf{Stone}$ establishes an anti-equivalence between Boolean algebras (propositional syntax) and compact totally disconnected Hausdorff spaces (Stone spaces of models/points). Explain how Michael Makkai generalized this duality from propositional logic to first-order coherent logic by replacing Boolean algebras with small pretopoi $\mathcal{E}$ and Stone spaces with ultracategories of models $\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal{E})$. (Hint: Points/models in $\operatorname{Spec}(B)$ are 2-valued homomorphisms $B \to \{0, 1\}$; in coherent logic, models of a pretopos $\mathcal{E}$ are coherent/left-exact functors $\mathcal{E} \to \mathbf{Set}$ preserving finite disjoint coproducts and effective quotients)
https://people.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/papers/Conceptual.pdf
Makkai Conceptual Completeness and Ultracategories by Jacob Lurie
(Definition of Ultracategories and Ultraproducts) Define an ultracategory $\mathcal{C}$ in the sense of Makkai and Lurie. (Hint: An ultracategory is a category $\mathcal{C}$ equipped with an ultrastructure functor $\int_{\mathcal{U}}: \mathcal{C}^I \to \mathcal{C}$ for every set $I$ and every ultrafilter $\mathcal{U}$ on $I$, specifying ultraproducts $\prod_{\mathcal{U}} X_i$ that satisfy transitivity/coherence under Fubini-type iterations of ultrafilters and principal ultrafilter trivializations $\int_{\delta_i} (X_j)_{j \in I} \cong X_i$)
https://people.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/papers/Conceptual.pdf
Makkai Conceptual Completeness and Ultracategories by Jacob Lurie
(Ultrafunctors and Symmetries of Ultraproducts) Define an ultrafunctor $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}$ between ultracategories. (Hint: $F$ is a functor equipped with coherent natural isomorphisms $F\left(\int_{\mathcal{U}} X_i\right) \cong \int_{\mathcal{U}} F(X_i)$ commuting with all ultraproduct operations)
https://people.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/papers/Conceptual.pdf
Makkai Conceptual Completeness and Ultracategories by Jacob Lurie
(Makkai's Conceptual Completeness Theorem) State Makkai's Conceptual Completeness Theorem as formulated by Lurie: for any small pretopos $\mathcal{E}$, let $\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal{E}) = \operatorname{Coh}(\mathcal{E}, \mathbf{Set})$ be its category of models equipped with its canonical ultracategory structure via pointwise ultraproducts in $\mathbf{Set}$. Prove that the evaluation functor $$\operatorname{ev}: \mathcal{E} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbf{Ult}(\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal{E}), \mathbf{Set})$$ is an equivalence of categories between the small pretopos $\mathcal{E}$ and the category of ultrafunctors from $\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal{E})$ to $\mathbf{Set}$. (Hint: This proves that a coherent first-order theory $\mathcal{E}$ is entirely and uniquely recoverable from its category of models together with the ultraproduct operations on those models)
https://people.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/papers/Conceptual.pdf
Makkai Conceptual Completeness and Ultracategories by Jacob Lurie
(Ultrastructures as Categorical Integration / Stokes' Formula) Detail Lurie's formulation of ultrastructures as a family of categorical integration operations. (Hint: Think of ultrafilters as $\{0, 1\}$-valued finitely additive measures $\mathcal{U}: \mathcal{P}(I) \to \{0, 1\}$; the ultraproduct functor $\int_{\mathcal{U}}: \mathcal{C}^I \to \mathcal{C}$ acts as an integration operator with respect to $\mathcal{U}$, and the coherence axioms mirror Fubini's theorem and Stokes'-type boundary-compatibility conditions on ultracategories)
https://people.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/papers/Conceptual.pdf
Makkai Conceptual Completeness and Ultracategories by Jacob Lurie
(Stone Duality as a Chu Construction / *-Autonomous Duality) Explain how Stone duality and Gödel's completeness theorem can be viewed through the lens of the Chu construction over $\mathbf{Set}$ with dualizing object $2 = \{0, 1\}$. (Hint: A Chu space $(\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{X}, e)$ pairs a syntactic object $\mathcal{A}$ with a semantic space $\mathcal{X}$ via an evaluation pairing $e: \mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{X} \to \{0, 1\}$; in Stone duality, $\mathcal{A}$ is a Boolean algebra, $\mathcal{X} = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Bool}}(\mathcal{A}, 2)$ is the set of prime filters/models, and the bidual evaluation $\mathcal{A} \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Stone}}(\operatorname{Spec}(\mathcal{A}), 2)$ is an isomorphism of *-autonomous systems)
https://people.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/papers/Conceptual.pdf
Makkai Conceptual Completeness and Ultracategories by Jacob Lurie
(Ultrafilters as Codensity Monads and Leinster's Heuristic) State Tom Leinster's theorem characterizing the ultrafilter monad $\beta: \mathbf{Set} \to \mathbf{Set}$ as the codensity monad of the inclusion functor $\mathbf{FinSet} \hookrightarrow \mathbf{Set}$. (Hint: The Stone–Čech compactification $\beta(X)$ is the maximal compactification of a discrete set $X$; integrating a bounded or finite-image function $f: X \to \mathbb{R}$ against an ultrafilter $\mathcal{U} \in \beta(X)$ picks out the unique value $r \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $f^{-1}(r) \in \mathcal{U}$, acting as an ultra-mode / point-evaluation on large sets)
https://people.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/papers/Conceptual.pdf
Makkai Conceptual Completeness and Ultracategories by Jacob Lurie
(Connections to Condensed Mathematics and Liquid Vector Spaces) How does Makkai's ultracategory framework relate to Clausen–Scholze condensed mathematics? (Hint: Condensed sets are sheaves on the pro-étale site of a point, testable against extremally disconnected compact Hausdorff spaces $\beta I$; in Makkai's framework, ultraproducts $\prod_{\mathcal{U}} X_i$ handle infinite limits and compact projections without topological pathologies, providing an alternate categorical path to measure theory and liquid vector spaces via ultrafilter integration)
https://people.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/papers/Conceptual.pdf

Entropy
(Categorical Characterization of Entropy: Baez-Fritz-Leinster) Let $\mathbf{FinProb}$ be the category of finite probability spaces $(X, P)$, where morphisms $f: (X, P) \to (Y, Q)$ are measure-preserving maps ($Q(y) = \sum_{x \in f^{-1}(y)} P(x)$). State the Baez–Fritz–Leinster theorem characterizing information loss $L(f) = S(P) - S(Q)$: prove that any functor $L: \mathbf{FinProb} \to (\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}, +)$ satisfying convex linearity $L(\lambda f \oplus (1-\lambda) g) = \lambda L(f) + (1-\lambda) L(g)$ and continuity is a constant non-negative multiple of the Shannon information loss. (Hint: Adapt the axioms to Tsallis entropy by replacing convex linearity with $q$-deformed non-extensive convex combinations)
https://www.its.caltech.edu/~matilde/EntropySlides2021Ma148.pdf
Entropy
(Information Geometry and the Fisher-Rao Metric) On a statistical manifold $\mathcal{M} = \{P_\theta = (p_1(\theta), \dots, p_n(\theta))\}$, define the Fisher–Rao information metric $g_{ij}(\theta) = \sum_{k=1}^n \frac{1}{p_k(\theta)} \frac{\partial p_k}{\partial \theta^i} \frac{\partial p_k}{\partial \theta^j} = \mathbb{E}_\theta \left[ \frac{\partial \log p}{\partial \theta^i} \frac{\partial \log p}{\partial \theta^j} \right]$. Show that the coordinate transformation $X_k = \sqrt{p_k}$ embeds $\mathcal{M}$ isometrically into a positive Euclidean sphere $S^{n-1}$ with metric $ds^2 = 4 \sum dX_k^2$. (Hint: Show that the Fisher–Rao metric is the Hessian of the Kullback–Leibler divergence: $g_{ij}(\theta) = \left. \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta_1^i \partial \theta_2^j} D_{\text{KL}}(P_{\theta_1} \parallel P_{\theta_2}) \right|_{\theta_1 = \theta_2 = \theta}$)
https://www.its.caltech.edu/~matilde/EntropySlides2021Ma148.pdf
Entropy
(Frobenius Manifolds and Statistical Quantum Cohomology) Define a Frobenius manifold $(M, g, \Phi)$ following Dubrovin and Manin, where $g$ is a flat metric and $\Phi$ is a potential function satisfying the WDVV (Witten–Dijkgraaf–Verlinde–Verlinde) associativity equations: $c_{ijk} = \frac{\partial^3 \Phi}{\partial t^i \partial t^j \partial t^k}$ defines an associative, commutative multiplication $\circ$ on the tangent bundle $TM$. Explain how statistical manifolds equipped with Amari–Chentsov cubic tensors $C(\partial_i, \partial_j, \partial_k) = \mathbb{E}\left[\partial_i \log p \cdot \partial_j \log p \cdot \partial_k \log p\right]$ connect to Frobenius structures in Gromov–Witten theory
https://www.its.caltech.edu/~matilde/EntropySlides2021Ma148.pdf
Entropy
(Hochschild Cohomology of Information Structures: Vigneaux's Theorem) Let $\mathcal{S}$ be the category of observables (random variables on finite probability spaces) with morphisms given by joint measurements / refinements. Define the Hochschild cochain complex $C^n(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{F}) = \operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{S}^{\otimes n}, \mathcal{F})$ for an information structure. State Pierre Baudot and Juan-Pablo Vigneaux's theorem: 1. The 0-th Hochschild cohomology $H^0(\mathcal{S}, \mathbb{R}) \cong \mathbb{R}$ when $\alpha = 1$, and vanishes otherwise. 2. The 1-cocycles $Z^1(\mathcal{S}, \mathbb{R})$ satisfying the cocycle condition $F(X \vee Y) = F(X) + F(Y \mid X)$ (the entropy chain rule) are spanned uniquely by the Shannon entropy (for extensive additivity) and by the Tsallis entropy $S_\alpha$ (for non-extensive deformations). (Hint: The entropy chain rule is the 1-cocycle condition in the Hochschild complex of the information algebra)
https://www.its.caltech.edu/~matilde/EntropySlides2021Ma148.pdf

The Moment Map and Equivariant Cohomology by Atiyah and Bott

Show that the modified symplectic 2-form $\widetilde{\omega}(X) = \omega + \langle \mu, X \rangle$ is an equivariantly closed form in the Cartan model. (Hint: Compute $d_G \widetilde{\omega}(X) = (d - \iota_{X_M})(\omega + \langle \mu, X \rangle) = d\omega - \iota_{X_M}\omega + d\langle \mu, X \rangle$; verify that this vanishes identically using $d\omega = 0$ and Hamilton's equation $d\langle \mu, X \rangle = \iota_{X_M}\omega$)

The Moment Map and Equivariant Cohomology by Atiyah and Bott

(Hint: For isolated fixed points $p \in M^G$, the integral over $M$ localizes completely to the fixed-point set: $\int_M \alpha(X) = \sum_{p \in M^G} \frac{\alpha(X)(p)}{\det\left(\frac{1}{2\pi} L_p(X)\right)}$, where $L_p(X) \in \mathfrak{so}(T_p M)$ is the infinitesimal rotation induced by $X \in \mathfrak{g}$ on the tangent space)

(Hint: For an $S^1$-action on a symplectic manifold $(M, \omega)$ with moment map $H$, the Fourier transform of the Liouville pushforward measure $\int_M e^{i t H} \frac{\omega^n}{n!}$ is evaluated exactly by the localized sum over the critical points of $H$, which are the fixed points of the circle action)

The Moment Map and Equivariant Cohomology by Atiyah and Bott

(Hint: The coefficient ring is $H^*(BS^1; \mathbb{Q}) \cong \mathbb{Q}[u]$ (a PID). Every finitely generated module over $\mathbb{Q}[u]$ decomposes into a free part and a torsion part; localizing by inverting the polynomial generator $u$ kills all $\mathbb{Q}[u]$-torsion supported outside the fixed-point set $M^{S^1}$, establishing an isomorphism $H_{S^1}^*(M) \otimes_{\mathbb{Q}[u]} \mathbb{Q}[u, u^{-1}] \cong H^*(M^{S^1}) \otimes \mathbb{Q}[u, u^{-1}]$)
